subject: Climate & Environment
title: Public Transit and Emissions
description: Learn Public Transit and Emissions in one minute.

hook.text: A full subway train removes roughly 800 cars from the road. Every single trip.

buildup.text: Bus rapid transit systems carry millions daily in cities like Curitiba, Bogotá, and Istanbul.

discovery.text: Per passenger kilometer, public transit produces 80% fewer emissions than a single-occupant car.

twist.text: Many US cities dismantled their streetcar systems in the 1950s to make room for highways.

climax.text: Investing in transit doesn't just cut emissions — it reduces congestion, saves time, and creates jobs.

punchline.text: A bus pass does more for the planet than most people realize.

quiz.question: How many fewer emissions does public transit produce per passenger km compared to a car?

details.summary: Public transit systems produce far fewer emissions per passenger-kilometer than private cars. Buses, trains, and metros move large numbers of people efficiently, reducing congestion and freeing urban land from roads and parking. Electrifying transit fleets can reduce emissions nearly to zero.
details.whyItMatters: Investing in public transit is one of the fastest ways to cut urban transport emissions while improving mobility for people who cannot drive or afford cars.
takeaways: Transit produces a fraction of car emissions per passenger-km
Buses and trains reduce congestion and road infrastructure needs
Electrification of fleets pushes transit emissions toward zero

faq.question: How much carbon does transit save compared to driving?
faq.answer: A full bus emits about a tenth of the CO2 per passenger-kilometer compared to single-occupancy cars. Electric metro systems produce even less when powered by clean grids. Shifting just 10 percent of car trips to transit significantly cuts a city's transport emissions.

faq.question: What is bus rapid transit?
faq.answer: BRT uses dedicated lanes, prepaid boarding, and frequent service to mimic metro-level performance at a fraction of the cost. Cities like Bogota, Curitiba, and Istanbul have built BRT systems that move hundreds of thousands of passengers daily.
